titre_video: Foreign Nations JUST Left the US Bond Market. Wall Street Panics RIGHT NOW.

segments.titre: Hook: China walked away, debt interest exceeds defense
segments.resume: The video opens by saying China no longer holds the debt headlines suggest. Western powers now spend more on interest than on defense, trillions of unbuyable bonds are flooding markets, and a shadowy private buyer is stepping in. A single margin call could pull the plug on the global economy.
segments.texte: Headlines scream about China owning America’s debt. Except… they walked away years ago. Right now, Western superpowers are spending more cash just paying interest than on their entire defense budgets. Trillions of unbuyable bonds are flooding the markets, causing the financial system to grind to a halt, forcing a shadowy private buyer to step into the vacuum. The global economy is on life support. And it only takes one single margin call to pull the plug.

segments.titre: August 2026 30-year Treasury auction at 5.216%
segments.resume: The US Treasury sold $25 billion of 30-year bonds at a 5.216% yield in late August 2026, the highest since 2001. Treasury yields shape corporate credit and mortgage rates worldwide. The government placed its debt, but the question is who buys from a country with $40 trillion of debt.
segments.texte: In late August, 2026, the United States Treasury sold $25 billion in 30 year bonds at a 5.216% yield. That’s the highest borrowing rate since 2001. And that’s important. Because when US Treasury bonds rates spike like this, the shockwaves rip through the entire global economy. That’s how influential American bonds are. They dictate everything from corporate credit rates to monthly mortgage payments, at home and abroad. The government successfully dumped its debt this time around, but who is buying bonds from a country drowning in $40 trillion of debt?

segments.titre: US national debt growth from 2 centuries to $40 trillion
segments.resume: It took over two centuries and two world wars to reach $1 trillion of debt. Debt neared $20 trillion in January 2017 and has more than doubled in under a decade, reaching $40 trillion in August 2026. The government now adds about a trillion dollars every 5 months.
segments.texte: The U.S. hit that astronomical tally in August 2026. It took over 2 centuries, including 2 world wars, to hit a trillion of national debt. By January 2017, that number had soared to almost $20 trillion. That figure has more than doubled less than a decade later. These days, the US government effectively adds another trillion dollars to its balance sheet every 5 months, on average.

segments.titre: Debt-to-GDP ratio and $1 trillion interest bill
segments.resume: The debt-to-GDP ratio of over 124% is among the worst in the world, alongside Japan, Sudan, Venezuela and Greece. Annual interest payments have crossed $1 trillion, more than the whole national defense budget, without reducing the principal.
segments.texte: It’s an eyewatering sum. But the “debt to GDP ratio” is even more concerning. That number compares a country’s total national debt to its gross domestic product (GDP). It basically shows how capable a country is of paying back the money it owes. America’s debt exceeds 124% of its GDP. It’s one of the worst ratios on Earth. Only a few select countries rank lower, including Japan, Sudan, Venezuela, and Greece. And it only gets worse from there. The annual interest payments alone on America’s debt have now crossed the $1 trillion mark. The US would have to spend more than its entire national defense budget every single year just to cover the interest costs on the debt it owes. And that’s without making a dent in the debt itself.

segments.titre: G7 nations spend more on debt interest than defense
segments.resume: A Bloomberg report shows most G7 nations spend more on debt interest than on defense: Italy 193%, the UK 105%, France 103%. The US is in a more dangerous position because of the sheer size of its debt.
segments.texte: Of course, America isn’t the only country in this sort of situation. A Bloomberg report revealed that most of the G7 nations are spending more on debt interest than defense. The numbers are staggering. Italy spends 193% of its defense budget on debt interest, for example. The UK pays 105%, and France hits 103%. But the U.S. is in a more dangerous position.

segments.titre: Traditional buyers: central banks and why they bought Treasuries
segments.resume: For decades US debt was the safe place to store capital, bought first by central banks of China, Japan, Western Europe and the Gulf States. Treasuries kept currencies under control against the dollar, stabilized trade prices and offered instant liquidity, so these countries bought hundreds of billions.
segments.texte: No other nation comes close to the US when it comes to the absolute enormity of the country’s overall debt. For decades, the global financial system operated according to an unwritten but all-important rule: US debt was the safest place to store capital. Whenever Washington DC decided to issue some fresh debt, the same familiar faces were happy to snap it up in large amounts. First in line were the Central Banks from countries like China, Japan, Western European powerhouses, and the Gulf States. Buying US bonds was an obvious move that made absolute economic sense, both in the short term and from a big picture perspective. It also helped them keep the values of their own currencies under control against the dollar. It also helped keep export and import prices sustainable. Bonds provided instant liquidity, since they could be sold, traded, and cashed in at any time. But the longer central banks were able to hold onto them, the more value they could feasibly make from their investments. So, these countries had no problem swallowing up hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of Treasuries.

segments.titre: Federal Reserve, pension funds and the cracking foundation
segments.resume: The Federal Reserve bought Treasuries to influence rates, and pension funds and insurers absorbed the rest. This demand raised bond prices, lowered yields and made it easier to finance the budget. The video says this foundation is now cracking.
segments.texte: But foreign powers weren’t the only ones soaking up America’s debt. The Federal Reserve also weaponized the system. They bought up billions of Treasuries to influence interest rates and prop up the economy. Whatever debt was left was hoovered up by pension funds and insurance giants. They all provided the stable foundation for American debt. It helped to increase the price of bonds while lowering their yields. That made it easier for the US government to finance its budget and spend on defense, infrastructure and education. But now, that foundation is cracking. The American economy is beginning to crumble.

segments.titre: Foreign central banks retreat: China halves its holdings
segments.resume: Japan remains the top foreign creditor with over $1 trillion and the UK holds $900 billion, but China has cut from a peak of $1.3 trillion to $633 billion. Foreign governments held about 40% of US debt around 2008 and only 12% now.
segments.texte: The foreign Central Banks haven’t bailed out entirely, but they’re heading towards… at speed. While Japan is still America’s largest foreign creditor, with over a trillion dollars’ worth of Treasuries. The UK holds another $900 billion in bonds. But other major players are getting out while they can. Chief among them is China. It used to be the second biggest holder of American debt and peaked at around $1.3 trillion. Today, it holds about half of that: $633 billion, to be exact. And it’s not a one-off. It’s just one part of a larger trend. Central Banks around the world have been slashing their holdings of US debt over the last couple of decades. Around the time of the 2008 financial crisis, foreign governments held around 40% of American debt. These days, it’s 12%. These countries didn’t just ease up a little on their investments;

segments.titre: Pension funds stop buying 30-year Treasuries
segments.resume: Pension funds used to buy 30-year Treasuries to guarantee retiree payouts. The shift from defined-benefit pensions to 401(k)s frees them from low-yield Treasuries, so they move into private equity and high-yield credit.
segments.texte: they dropped off dramatically. They weren’t the only ones. The pension funds started pulling out, too. For years, they’d been so reliable. In order to provide the guaranteed monthly payouts they promised to retirees, these funds had no other choice but to buy 30-year Treasury bonds. They could always be counted on to take their share of America’s debt. But there’s been a shift in corporate America. People are turning their backs on defined-benefit pensions and towards systems, like 401(k)s. And with 401(k)s proving more popular and appealing, pension funds no longer need to tie up their investments in low-yield 30-year Treasuries. They can focus on making the most money out of private equity and high-yield credit, instead.

segments.titre: Vanishing buyers force yields up; Bessent steps in
segments.resume: The Treasury must sell about $2 trillion of new debt each year plus refinance maturing debt. With demand falling, it raises rates, and in August 2026 long-term yields hit 20-year highs, threatening mortgage rates. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had to act.
segments.texte: The timing couldn’t be worse. The US government is setting new records for national debt. Its interest payments are spiraling out of control. And it needs buyers who are willing to buy-in to bonds for an extended period of time. Now those buyers are vanishing. Every year the Treasury needs to offload $2 trillion of fresh debt it accumulates each year. It also has to refinance the trillions of pre-existing debt as it approaches its expiry date. When demand drops, the Treasury has one move left: to jack up interest rates to attract buyers. In August 2026, long-term Treasury yields reached highs that hadn’t been seen in over 20 years. Tens of millions of American homeowners suddenly faced the very real threat of sudden mortgage rate spikes to match. The Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, had to step in and take drastic action to control the situation.

segments.titre: Bond buybacks and T-bill flooding as a desperate move
segments.resume: Bessent announced Washington would double bond buybacks, financed by flooding the market with short-term Treasury bills. The video compares it to paying one credit card with several smaller ones. It signalled that the sovereign bond market was broken and manipulated.
segments.texte: To calm the panicking markets, Bessent announced that Washington would double its bond buybacks. To foot the bill, Washington is flooding the market with short term Treasury bills that mature in months, not years. It was a desperate move. It was like paying off a credit card with a handful of smaller cards. While it provided some short-term relief, it came at a massive cost. Washington admitted to the world that the sovereign bond market was broken. The government was having to artificially manipulate the system just to keep the lights on. So if pension funds and foreign Central Banks

segments.titre: Hedge funds become buyers; Basel III removes bank shock absorbers
segments.resume: The new buyers are hyper-leveraged private macro hedge funds. After 2008, Basel III forced banks like Bank of America and JP Morgan to hold large cash reserves and limit leverage, so they stopped absorbing Treasury auctions, just as debt exploded.
segments.texte: aren’t buying up US debt anymore, who is? A collective of hyper-leveraged, private, macro hedge funds. And they’re following an extremely dangerous trading strategy. To stop another financial meltdown like the 2008 crisis, financial regulators issued a new rulebook called Basel III. Under these rules, giants like the Bank of America and JP Morgan were told they had to have vast cash reserves available at all times. They couldn’t take huge risks and leverage their capital like they had before. It brought some kind of stability to the banking sector. But it also had a vicious knock-on effect on the global financial system. Before the rule change, big banks acted like the shock absorbers for American debt. When the Treasury auctioned off billions in bonds, the banks swallowed the supply into their own balance sheets. Then they distributed the funds to investors around the world. The new rules changed that. The shock absorbers were gone. Again, the timing couldn’t have been worse. Right as US debt was exploding, banks were being handcuffed. It’s not profitable for banks to hold such huge amounts of debt, so other entities had to step in and fill the void.

segments.titre: Hedge funds vs. long-term holders: profit-driven buyers
segments.resume: Hedge funds are not bound by Basel III or leverage limits and go wherever returns are. Unlike central banks and pension funds, they are not long-term holders and may sell within months, days or hours.
segments.texte: The hedge funds. They don’t need to worry about Basel III or other regulations. They don’t need to concern themselves with leverage limits or arbitrary authorities. They have more freedom to put their money wherever they want it… as long as it provides a reasonable return. That’s the big difference between these funds – the new owners of American debt – and the central banks and pension funds that came before them. They’re not in this for the long haul. They’re in it for profit.

segments.titre: How the cash-futures basis trade works
segments.resume: The basis trade exploits a tiny price gap between a physical Treasury bond and its futures contract. The fund buys the cheaper physical bond and shorts the futures contract, locking in a risk-free profit on both sides.
segments.texte: That means they’re happy to cash out within months, weeks, days, or even hours after buying in. As long as they’re in a better position, that’s all that matters. To make sure they end up winning, they rely on a financial mechanism known as the cash-futures basis trade, or basis trade, for short. On paper, a physical U.S. bond and a bond futures contract should cost the same amount. But they don’t. The futures contracts are often a micro-fraction more expensive. For you, the difference is worthless. But for hedge funds gambling on billions of dollars, that micro-fraction of a penny adds up to huge profits. That’s where the basis trade comes in. If a hedge fund sees that a physical 30-year bond is trading at a tiny discount compared to a 30-year futures contract, they buy the physical bond. Meanwhile, they short, or sell, the corresponding contract. They lock in both sides, creating a risk free profit.

segments.titre: Repo leverage: recycling bonds into more debt
segments.resume: Funds pledge the purchased bond as collateral in the repo market for near-zero-interest cash, then repeat the trade over and over. From 2023 to September 2025 hedge fund Treasury holdings reached $4 trillion and the basis trade $830 billion.
segments.texte: But to make it really lucrative, they use a loophole called the “Repo” market. The hedge fund takes the freshly purchased bond straight to a bank, which accepts it as collateral. Then, the bank hands over cash at near zero interest. But instead of pocketing it, the hedge fund buys another bond, shorts another contract and uses the new bond to borrow more money. They do this over and over again. They borrow more and more cash to supercharge their investment and profits. By recycling the same capital numerous times, they rack up an enormous amount of debt. Without anyone noticing, these funds have been using the Repo Market to swallow the debt Washington dumps into the market. And it adds up. Between 2023 and September 2025, hedge funds’ Treasury investments grew to a staggering $4 trillion. Meanwhile, the cash-futures basis trade alone reached $830 billion. The global monetary system is being part-financed

segments.titre: Repo spike risk: forced liquidation and a frozen market
segments.resume: The hedge funds bet on stable repo markets. A sudden repo rate spike would make the basis trade self-destruct, forcing funds to sell bonds and buy back futures. Bond prices would crash, yields surge, margin calls cascade, and no buyers would exist, freezing the US debt market.
segments.texte: by a tiny cabal of private funds operating with the kind of leverage that would terrify even the most grizzled Wall Street investor. These hedge funds are banking everything on repo markets remaining stable. As long as that happens, the game continues. DC can keep dumping its debt and hedge funds can keep on pocketing their profits. But the second something changes – like a sudden, unexpected spike in repo rates– the whole basis trade self-destructs. And if that happens, hedge funds can’t ease their way out of the market. They have to evacuate ASAP. It means liquidating their positions immediately. They have to sell off their physical bonds and buy back their futures contracts. If dozens of funds all did that at the same time, cashing in hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of Treasuries overnight, it would be catastrophic. Bond prices would crash. Yields would surge. And waves of automated margin calls would be triggered to the very same hedge funds. They’d have to sell off even more Treasuries in a market that is increasingly running out of buyers. Foreign central banks wouldn’t want them. Neither would pension funds. Even primary American banks wouldn’t be able to step in and save the day due to the Basel III regulations. What happens next? The market for US debt screeches to a frightening halt.

segments.titre: Precedent: March 2020 basis trade breakdown and Fed rescue
segments.resume: In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, the basis trade broke down, margin calls hit hedge funds and they dumped bonds. Banks could not absorb the supply, Treasury and credit markets nearly collapsed, and the Fed injected over a trillion dollars and bought bonds.
segments.texte: And it’s not impossible as it sounds. It’s happened once before. Back in 2020, when the drama of the COVID-19 pandemic was still unfolding, the basis trade broke down. Investors run for the exits, and automated margin calls were triggered on futures positions of the wealthiest hedge funds all across America. To raise the money they needed to survive, they dumped bonds. Lots of them. The big banks couldn’t afford to buy the sudden surge of government debt. The Treasury market suffered a brief but shocking breakdown. Credit and mortgage markets were pushed to the brink of collapse until the Federal Reserve stepped in to contain the crisis. Resorting to some of the most drastic economic measures in modern history, the Fed funneled more than a trillion dollars into the system. They promised to buy up huge swathes of bonds, giving the hedge funds the buyers they so sorely needed. A crisis had been averted.

segments.titre: Regulators failed to rein in the basis trade
segments.resume: After 2020 regulators did not take action to control the basis trade, effectively letting hedge funds take even more reckless risks, and the consequences are being seen now.
segments.texte: But the foundations were already being laid for the next one. And regulators failed to learn their lesson. They didn’t take action to bring the basis trade under control. Instead, they effectively allowed hedge funds to get away with even more reckless spending. And we’re seeing the consequences play out now.

segments.titre: Basis trade moves offshore to the Cayman Islands
segments.resume: An October 2025 Federal Reserve Board report found hedge funds moved much of their business to offshore havens like the Cayman Islands, escaping taxes and regulation. The engine financing US debt now runs outside US jurisdiction.
segments.texte: As Washington’s debt spirals, the basis trade is worth more than ever before. But the infrastructure underpinning this mechanism has migrated beyond America’s borders. An October 2025 report from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve revealed hedge funds had moved much of their business to offshore tax havens, like the Cayman Islands. And they can enjoy a whole lot of benefits, like escaping corporate income tax and capital gains tax. More importantly, the regulatory freedom allows investors to set up highly leveraged trading vehicles without anyone asking questions. That means the engine funding America’s debt is running completely outside the U.S. government's jurisdiction.

segments.titre: No easy solutions: the Fed cannot fix the next break
segments.resume: The Fed cannot easily step in when offshore basis trades collapse. Debt exceeds $40 trillion and interest over $1 trillion. Raising rates to fight inflation makes refinancing costlier, while Washington relies on short-term, profit-hungry hedge funds.
segments.texte: The next time the basis trade falls apart – which is almost inevitable – the Fed can’t step in and put out the fire with a quick fix solution. And with every day that passes, the world draws closer to that financial doomsday scenario. The numbers are all moving in the wrong direction. Debt has crossed $40 trillion. Annual interest payments alone exceed $1 trillion. DC is in a nosedive so steep that there’s almost no way to pull up and avoid a crash. Every prospective solution creates additional problems. The Fed can raise interest rates to calm inflation. But that just makes maturing debt even more expensive to refinance. And with the conventional stable buyers – like foreign central banks and pension funds – edging out of the market, Washington is becoming reliant on short term, profit hungry hedge fund traders. And it’s the whole world that will pay.

segments.titre: Global fallout when the trade breaks
segments.resume: When the trade breaks, leveraged sell orders cascade automatically and positions are liquidated at once. Central banks must intervene as borrowing costs, mortgage rates and corporate balance sheets are hit worldwide, with no way back.
segments.texte: When the trade breaks, a cascade of leveraged sell orders will automatically execute. Positions will be liquidated immediately. Central banks will be forced to make emergency interventions as chaos tears through borrowing costs, mortgage rates, and corporate balance sheets worldwide. Once that financial trigger has been pulled, there is no putting the bullet back in the chamber.

segments.titre: Outro: financial system hanging by a thread
segments.resume: The video closes by saying the US financial system hangs by a thread and points viewers to a follow-up video, 'What If The US Economy CRASHES', on the fallout.
segments.texte: The U.S. financial system is hanging by a thread. But what if it snaps? Watch ‘What If The US Economy CRASHES’ to find out how bad the fallout would be. Or click on this.
